source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In a Cameroonian village, a well or a spring is a meeting place where news is exchanged, and a death in the family is marked by days of mourning and the whole community gathering. The fourth Gospel contains two scenes of this kind, Jesus talking to a woman at a well and Jesus at the tomb of his friend Lazarus. Examiners often take their questions from these stories, from the wider themes in John and from the attitude of Jesus towards Jewish teaching. This course gives the facts and shows how to turn them into a 25-mark answer.

items: The New Testament has four Gospels. Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material, and John differs in content and style.
Christians believe that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah (Christ) and the Son of God, and that he rose from the dead.
Jesus and his first disciples were Jews, and the Gospel records disputes between Jesus and some religious leaders in his time.

sections.titre: John's Gospel: character, signs and key encounters
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Character and purpose
Christian tradition attributes the fourth Gospel to John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, though scholars discuss its authorship. The Gospel states its purpose in John 20:31: that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name. Its prologue (John 1) presents Jesus as the Word, who was with God, was God and became flesh. Much of John is unique to it: the wedding at Cana, Nicodemus, the woman at the well, the raising of Lazarus, the washing of the disciples' feet and the long farewell teaching of John 13 to 17. It uses *signs* (miracles that point to who Jesus is) and *I am* sayings. It has no parables like the Sower or the Good Samaritan, but it develops extended images such as the shepherd and the vine.

### Signs and I am sayings
| Signs (traditionally seven) | I am sayings |
|---|---|
| Water into wine at Cana (John 2) | The bread of life (John 6) |
| Healing of the official's son (John 4) | The light of the world (John 8) |
| Healing of the paralysed man (John 5) | The door and the good shepherd (John 10) |
| Feeding of the crowd (John 6) | The resurrection and the life (John 11) |
| Walking on the sea (John 6) | The way, the truth and the life (John 14) |
| Healing of the man born blind (John 9) | The true vine (John 15) |
| Raising of Lazarus (John 11) | |

### Jesus and the woman at the well (John 4)
Jesus, tired from the journey, sits at Jacob's well near the Samaritan town of Sychar and asks a woman for water, crossing the barriers between Jews and Samaritans, and between men and women. He speaks of living water, shows knowledge of her life, and teaches that true worship is in spirit and truth. He tells her that he is the Messiah, and she goes to tell the townspeople, many of whom come to believe.

### The raising of Lazarus (John 11)
Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, dies. Jesus arrives when he has been in the tomb four days, declares that he is the resurrection and the life, weeps and calls Lazarus out of the tomb. The event leads the leaders to plot Jesus' death. Christians read it as a sign pointing to Jesus' own resurrection, but there are differences: Lazarus emerges still wrapped in grave clothes and will die again.

variantes.nom: Question on an incident (comment on, examine the story of...)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a named passage is given, such as the well at Sychar or Lazarus.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Summarise the setting in two sentences, identify the main teaching (identity of Jesus, belief, life), and connect it to the Gospel's purpose in John 20:31. Do not retell every detail.

variantes.nom: Question on Jesus and Jewish teaching (with reference to two examples)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked about Jesus' attitude to the law, the Sabbath, the Temple or the Scriptures.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose two examples with chapters (for instance a healing on the Sabbath in John 5 or 9, and the claim that the Scriptures bear witness to him in John 5). Show that Jesus respects and fulfils Jewish tradition but disagrees with some leaders' interpretation, then give a judgement.

sections.enonce_markdown: Examine the raising of Lazarus as a sign in John's Gospel.

etapes.justification: Examine means look at the event carefully and judge its meaning.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: (1) the event, (2) what it reveals about Jesus, (3) the reactions, (4) link to the resurrection.
Lazarus of Bethany dies; Jesus arrives after four days, weeps, orders the stone to be removed and calls Lazarus out; he comes out wrapped in grave clothes (John 11).

etapes.justification: John calls miracles signs because they point beyond themselves.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Jesus says that he is the resurrection and the life, so the sign shows his power over death and invites belief, which fits the purpose of the Gospel in John 20:31.

etapes.justification: The effects are part of the meaning.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Many believed in him, but the leaders held a council and began to plot his death, so the sign also helps cause the events that lead to the cross.

etapes.action: Link to Jesus' own resurrection and give a judgement.
etapes.justification: Compare and contrast to avoid a one-sided claim.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Lazarus was raised to ordinary life and would die again, while Jesus' resurrection, as Christians believe, is to a new life. The raising is therefore a pointer to the resurrection, not the same event.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The raising of Lazarus is the last and greatest sign in John's Gospel. It shows Jesus as the resurrection and the life, calls for belief, and brings both faith and hostility. It points forward to Jesus' own resurrection but differs from it, since Lazarus returned to earthly life.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing the Lazarus of John 11 with the Lazarus of the parable in Luke 16.
items.pourquoi_faux: John's Lazarus is the brother of Martha and Mary, raised from the dead; Luke's Lazarus is a poor man in a story told by Jesus.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that John contains the same parables as Matthew, Mark and Luke.
items.pourquoi_faux: John uses signs, long discourses and I am sayings; it does not have the well-known parables of the other Gospels.
items.correction_markdown: Describe John's own style with examples from John 6, 10 and 15.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that Jesus rejected Jewish teaching completely.
items.pourquoi_faux: In John, Jesus attends Jewish feasts, appeals to the Scriptures and says that salvation is from the Jews (John 4), although he challenges some interpretations.
items.correction_markdown: Use words like 'fulfils' and 'reinterprets', and give two examples.

items.erreur_markdown: Treating the phrase 'the Jews' in John as meaning all Jewish people.
items.pourquoi_faux: Jesus and his disciples were Jews, and in John the phrase often refers to particular authorities who opposed him.
items.correction_markdown: Write 'some Jewish leaders' or 'the authorities' when describing conflicts.

items.erreur_markdown: Retelling the story of the woman at the well without commenting on it.
items.pourquoi_faux: A question asking you to comment needs an interpretation: what does the encounter show?
items.correction_markdown: Link each stage of the conversation (water, her life, worship, Messiah) to what it shows about Jesus.

items.enonce_markdown: List four of the I am sayings of Jesus in John's Gospel.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each correct saying with its theme: bread of life; light of the world; the door or good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth and the life; the true vine. **Any four.**

items.enonce_markdown: Explain the significance of the changing of water into wine at Cana (John 2).
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each developed point. It is the first of the signs, in which Jesus revealed his glory and the disciples believed. The water was in jars used for Jewish purification, so the change suggests that Jesus brings something new in the place of the old rites. The abundance of the wine suggests God's generosity. His mother's request and his answer that his hour had not yet come show that his work follows God's timing. **Significance: the sign reveals Jesus' identity and begins the call to faith.**

items.enonce_markdown: Assess the importance of the prologue (John 1:1 to 18) for the rest of the Gospel.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for a balanced argument. The prologue presents Jesus as the Word who was with God, was God and became flesh, so it states who Jesus is from the beginning. It introduces the themes of life, light, witness (John the Baptist), belief and rejection, which return in the signs, the I am sayings and the passion. It tells the reader in advance that some will receive him and some will not. It also shows that the Gospel presents Jesus as the one who reveals the Father. **Judgement: the prologue is the key to the Gospel because it gives the reader the viewpoint from which every later scene is told.**

items_markdown: John is traditionally ascribed to John the apostle, differs from the synoptic Gospels, and states its purpose in John 20:31.
John uses signs and I am sayings to show who Jesus is; the signs are traditionally counted as seven and end with the raising of Lazarus.
In John 4 Jesus talks with a Samaritan woman at a well, crosses social and religious barriers, teaches about living water and true worship, and reveals himself as the Messiah.
The raising of Lazarus (John 11) shows Jesus' power over death, points to his own resurrection and increases the leaders' opposition.
On Jesus and Jewish teaching, give two examples with chapters and argue that he fulfils and reinterprets tradition while criticising some leaders' readings.
